_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 3 Habitats. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in content/lesson-3.py part by part (what a habitat is; the pond; the desert and the Arctic; counting and graphing; looking after habitats), with one chapter for 2Be.03 and the pattern in the class's block graph (the lesson's 'Hot, cold, wet, dry' and 'Count and graph the animals' steps) placed between the last two parts. Pictures are the lesson's own: its four habitat drawings (ART.scene habitat 0-3, the demo's Next place frames), the kit's polar bear, seal, bottle, log and beetle, and the block graph of its graph step (teal blocks, one per animal: pond 8, garden 6, park 4, car park 1). The frog with legs, the rabbit's burrow, the garden and the car park are drawn by the film, because the lesson pictures them only as emoji. People are brown (renderer.skin).
title: Habitats
subtitle: Grade 2 Science
objectives: Know that an environment in which a plant or animal naturally lives is its habitat.
Know that different habitats contain different plants and animals.
Identify similarities and differences between local environments in terms of hot, cold, dry, wet, many plants, few plants, many animals and few animals.
Know that human activity can affect the environment.
Identify simple patterns in results, e.g. increasing and decreasing patterns.
Present and interpret results using tables and block graphs.
Talk about how science helps us understand our effect on the world around us.

beats.say: Where does a frog live? A camel? A deer? A polar bear?
Every plant and animal lives in the habitat that suits it.
A habitat is where a plant or animal naturally lives.
A pond is a habitat. So are a desert, a forest and the icy Arctic.
A pond gives a frog all it needs: water, insects, plants to hide in.
A rabbit sleeps in its burrow. The burrow is its home.
But its habitat is bigger: the burrow and the field it feeds in.
A pond is wet. Frogs, ducks, fish and water plants live there.
A frog's smooth skin and long legs suit a pond.
Suit means to be right for. Webbed feet suit a pond, too.
A frog needs water. The dry desert is a camel's habitat, not a frog's.
A desert is hot and dry. Camels, lizards and cactus plants live there.
A camel can go for days without water.
The Arctic is icy and very cold. Polar bears and seals live there.
A polar bear's thick fur keeps it warm.
Different habitats hold different animals. Each one suits its place.
Scientists count what lives in a habitat: six frogs, three ducks, eight fish.
A block graph has one block for each animal counted.
The tallest column shows the most: eight fish.
The shortest shows the least: three ducks. You see it at a glance.
Compare places. Is it hot or cold? Is it wet or dry?
Are there many plants and animals, or few?
A garden is wet after rain, with many plants. A car park is dry, with few.
A class counted animals in four places. The pond had eight. The car park had one.
Wetter places, with more plants, had more animals.
Rubbish in a pond can hurt the frogs and fish.
Cut down a forest, and the deer and the birds lose their habitat.
Planting flowers gives bees a habitat. A log pile gives beetles somewhere to live.
What people do changes habitats, for better or for worse. Science shows us how.
A habitat is where a living thing naturally lives. Each one suits its habitat.
Compare places: hot or cold, wet or dry, many or few.
A block graph shows the most and the least at a glance.
What we do changes habitats. So look after them!
